name: Anarchy
scope: Anarchy in the sense its defining sources give the word when they treat it as a political ideal: a society or political regime without rulers, state or authority, in which people govern themselves directly (Dupuis-Déri, s1: a fourth pure regime in which all rule by consensus, without an authority; Taylor, s4: doing without the state; Malatesta, s5: the state of a people without any constituted authority; Proudhon in s3: the absence of a sovereign). The pejorative sense (disorder, chaos, Hobbes's state of nature) is how critics use the word and is not followed; Dupuis-Déri calls chaos anarchy's degenerate form. Anarchism as a movement and philosophy, and its strands, are separate catalog ideologies and are not followed here; only what the sources say about anarchy itself counts.

keyFigures.role: Early advocate of anarchy as preferable to lasting despotism (Political Justice, 1793)

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet lists military institutions among those of the state that the abolition of government removes, and the soldier among its instruments.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet names the policeman, soldier, prison and tax collector as the indispensable instruments of government, which anarchy abolishes; Dupuis-Déri describes anarchy as a regime without a coercive branch, with neither state nor police.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: In Dupuis-Déri's account anarchy has no leader and all decide together through assemblies; a leader dealing directly with the people presupposes the leader anarchy excludes.

clerical-rule.rationale: In Dupuis-Déri's account anarchy has no authority at all, with all citizens deciding together by consensus; rule by senior scholars is an authority of a minority, a different regime.

conscription.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet counts enforcing military service among the powers of the governors that anarchy does away with.

corporate-influence.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet says the richest need not sit in government because they keep ministers and members of parliament dependent on them.

death-penalty.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet lists the power to judge and punish transgressors of the law among the powers of government that anarchy abolishes.

democracy-becomes-oligarchy.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet says universal suffrage leaves government the servant of the propertied class and elects those who best deceive the masses.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The source defines anarchy as having no leader and no official holding recognised authority, so choosing a head of state, however elected, contradicts it.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Dupuis-Déri defines anarchy as the absence of any leader, with all governing together by consensus; a ruler passing power to a child is monarchy, the opposite regime.

elective-rulers.rationale: Dupuis-Déri's anarchy has no leader at all, elected or not, since all govern themselves directly through consensual deliberation; an elected head of state is a leader.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Anarchy as Dupuis-Déri defines it has no leader and no coercive apparatus to impose its authority; a head of state commanding armed forces is both.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: The source defines anarchy by the absence of any leader or official authority; a head of state with powers over a parliament presupposes what anarchy excludes.

leader-cult.rationale: Anarchy is defined in the source by zero leaders, all ruling together; honouring a leader as the nation's embodiment has no place in it.

minority-veto.rationale: Dupuis-Déri says in anarchy a dissenter may block a decision or withdraw and be freed from the consensual process and its results; he adds that real consensus is not pure unanimity.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet counts kings among the governors whose power anarchy abolishes; Britannica quotes Proudhon's definition of anarchy as the absence of a sovereign.

natural-rulers.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet asks whether governors are exceptionally gifted men fit to act for all and answers that no one should hold government power, even the ablest.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet rejects government altogether, including its protective functions, which it says exist to defend the privileged; anarchy is society without government.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Stanford entry reports Wolff's argument that the state's commands never have binding moral force and create no duty of obedience, the philosophical anarchist position.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Anarchy is defined in the source as the absence of any leader, all governing together; a head of state, even above parties, is a leader.

one-party-rule.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet rejects government by any class or party, since the ideas and interests of the ruling party triumph and the others are sacrificed.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet lists members of parliament among the governors and calls parliamentary government a servant of the propertied class, to be abolished with all government.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Dupuis-Déri's anarchy has all citizens govern themselves directly through deliberation, with no delegation of power to a separate authority.

party-commands-army.rationale: Dupuis-Déri describes anarchy as self-government of all without an authority relying on a coercive apparatus; a ruling party commanding the armed forces is the opposite.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Anarchy as Dupuis-Déri defines it has no leader and no authority resting on coercion or subordination; authority bound by oaths of lords and followers is the opposite.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: Dupuis-Déri defines anarchy as self-government by consensual deliberation in which an assembly seeks consensus rather than a majority; the Stanford entry cites this as rule by all with consensus as the goal.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet says governors spend their energy keeping power and satisfying friends, and that all they undertake serves domination and the privileges of their class.

power-shapes-accepted-knowledge.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet says masters, priests and teachers interested in government's necessity teach that it is necessary, and that religion is propagated to defend political and economic privilege.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Dupuis-Déri defines anarchy by the absence of any leader or authority, rule by all together; a head of state treated as sacred contradicts that.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet aims at the destruction of every political institution based on authority and the constitution of a free society in its place.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet holds that no one should hold power to make laws and compel others; Britannica quotes Proudhon's definition of anarchy as the absence of a sovereign.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet says government's essential function in all times is to oppress and exploit the masses and defend the exploiters, an instrument of the dominant class.

state-harmful.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet defines anarchy as the state of a people without government and calls for destroying every political institution based on authority; Dupuis-Déri's anarchy is self-government without any authority resting on a coercive apparatus.

strong-leader.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet argues that even the ablest and best rulers would see their beneficial influence paralysed by holding power, and rejects rule by any individual.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet condemns the judge and policeman who force those who think differently to keep silent as part of the machinery anarchy abolishes.

total-state.rationale: Malatesta's pamphlet holds government harmful and unnecessary, and Dupuis-Déri's anarchy has no authority at all, so a state directing every area of life is its opposite.

summary: Anarchy, in the sense its defining sources give the word as a political ideal, is a society or regime without rulers, state or authority, in which people govern themselves directly. Dupuis-Déri treats it as a fourth pure regime run by consensual deliberation without a coercive apparatus, and Malatesta defines it as the state of a people without any constituted authority, with government abolished. The sources speak mainly about the state, rulers, coercion and how decisions are made, and say little on most economic or social questions.
